# Eshan Roy (eshanized)

> Systems Engineer, open-source builder, and infrastructure architect. Builds systems software, autonomous engineering runtimes, and developer tooling.

Eshan Roy (known online as eshanized) is an engineer and researcher who builds systems software, developer infrastructure, and open-source products. His work explores the intersection of systems engineering, Linux, and autonomous software engineering.

## Primary Projects

- [M31A](https://m31a.tonmoyinfrastructure.org): A Rust-native autonomous software-engineering runtime with non-bypassable policy gates and verifiable execution. The model proposes actions; the runtime enforces policy. Completed missions produce cryptographic SHA-256 evidence digests.
- [Snigdha OS](https://github.com/Snigdha-OS): An Arch-based Linux distribution ecosystem focused on a cohesive desktop experience, system tooling, package management, and developer utilities.
- [Octate](https://tonmoyinfrastructure.org/projects/octate): A terminal-native AI code review CLI combining local Tree-sitter WASM AST parsing, cross-file reference graphs, and static linter discovery with multi-stage LLM review DAGs.
- [SLMGen](https://github.com/eshanized): Small-language-model experimentation infrastructure for practical ML engineering, fine-tuning, and evaluation.
- [MCP SuperAssistant](https://github.com/eshanized): Developer tooling built around the Model Context Protocol ecosystem.

## Engineering Philosophy & Principles

- Architecture supports maintainability: Systems should be designed so that future maintainers can reason about them without indirection.
- Reliability is verified, not asserted: A model declaring success is not proof. Completion requires empirical evidence: clean compilers, passing tests, and verifiable digests.
- Developer experience is system design: Ergonomics, installation, and error reporting are architectural decisions made from the first commit.
- Open source should be useful and understandable: High-integrity documentation and honest status labels matter as much as the implementation.
- Automation needs boundaries and observability: Autonomous systems must fail closed through non-bypassable gates, with observable and recoverable execution states.
- Performance improvements require measurement: Improvements must be supported by empirical data rather than intuition.
